值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭露中國AI模型MiniMax爆發資料外洩事件的真相，以及其「零數據保留」（ZDR）認證遭OpenRouter撤銷的完整經過。
  • 深入分析中介API轉運平台如何利用技術漏洞偷換路由，以低價中國境內伺服器充當海外伺服器，使隱私承諾形同虛設的內幕。
  • 剖析中國法律規範（如網路日誌須保存六個月）與國際「零數據保留」資安標準之間的根本衝突，警示使用此類服務的隱私風險。

摘要

誘餌測試揭穿謊言：MiniMax零數據保留認證遭撤銷

作者指出，長期以來外界對中國大模型的資料隱私疑慮終於得到證實。資安機構研究員透過類似「釣魚標記」的手法，向多個AI模型發送了數百萬組隨機且唯一的單次網址。測試結果顯示，唯獨MiniMax模型在請求發出後的40至130小時、甚至數天後，其後台仍有第三方或系統持續存取這些網址。這項鐵證導致知名API聚合平台OpenRouter於11月21日向用戶發布警告信，直接點名並撤銷MiniMax的零數據保留（ZDR）標籤，明確指出使用該模型存在內容被非法留存的風險。

中介節點偷換路由：飛書群組驚現隱私洩漏足跡

作者進一步說明，許多API中介轉運商雖然標榜使用海外自建伺服器並承諾零數據保留，但為了賺取價差，往往會將用戶請求私下轉發到中國大陸較便宜的節點。在一次測試中，測試人員刻意選用了標註零保留的美國伺服器，但其唯一的測試網址卻在24天後出現在一個飛書群組中，且在兩分鐘內被來自北京與上海的6台不同設備點擊存取。此事件徹底撕破了中介商的承諾，OpenRouter隨後終止了與3家供應商的合作，並直接拔除了多達125個服務端點的ZDR認證。

法規與技術的衝突：在中國境內「零數據保留」實屬違法

作者從法律層面深入剖析，強調在中國境內追求真正的「零數據保留」在法律上根本不可行。根據中國《網絡安全法》規定，網路日誌必須強制保存至少六個月，以備官方調取；同時《生成式人工智能服務管理暫行辦法》也要求服務商落實內容審核機制，若發現違法違規內容更必須採取處置並主動上報。作者感嘆，中國境內大模型的高強度審查與法定數據留存義務，意味著用戶在這些模型上的輸入紀錄不但不可能被即時銷毀，使用者甚至可能因敏感輸入而已被通報給主管機關，隱私保障面臨極大挑戰。

================================================

# :00 警告信点名了谁

They all look down on me, and I’m the one who’s least capable. People have always worried about Chinese large models leaking data, and this time , it's finally been confirmed. Hello everyone, welcome to the YouTube channel sharing stories. First, the report that blew the lid off this was published by the security firm Drugles, stating they sent out a batch of links and discovered one Chinese AI company kept this information for post-review.

# :15 零数据留存承诺了什么

But strangely, the report didn’t name exactly who it was. Originally, they wanted to downplay it a bit and cover it up, but unexpectedly, on November 21st, the major token provider OpenRouter sent a letter to customers directly naming Minimax and stating their zero-data retention. license has been revoked; whenever anyone uses a Minimax model, your content is at risk of being retained.

# :25 张搜狐的电话从哪来

When sending a warning to customers, you have to be clear; you can't just hide it and say, "Oh, we found some Chinese AI is doing something wrong," right? You have to name names. So, what was stripped from Minimax and its related service providers this time ? It’s the zero-data retention tag, also known as the ZDR tag. What is zero-data retention? It means the information users input and all the information I output. I will delete it immediately after processing and will not store it locally.

# :09 一次性网址为何被访问

. Many models on OpenRouter originally had this tag. But it turned out that you had the tag, yet you didn't follow through; all the link information was being stored by you , and since it's confirmed and evidence has been found, you can no longer keep this label. As for other Chinese large models, some still carry this tag. So, how does Minimax explain this? So far, Minimax itself hasn't given any explanation; only some of their intermediary service providers have.

# :42 谁接单谁在跑模型

provided some. For example, a service provider called Streamlike said that before October 22nd , they were indeed performing content review. Later, they enabled data retention, but everyone please note: this zero-retention tag had been applied long ago, and they had promised it early on, even though they were doing content review all along. So, how was this detected? Do you remember a joke we used to tell? It’s the story of Zhang Hubao and Wang Jingdong; someone once wanted to see.

# :01 三家下架与端点撤标

exactly who was leaking their information. He logs into Sohu and registers a username called "Zhang Sohu." He logs into Taobao, registers a username called "Li Taobao," and logs into JD, calling himself "Wang Jingdong." Later, someone calls him: "Hello, we are looking for a student named Zhang Sohu, is he there?" It doesn't matter exactly who at Sohu leaked the information; what matters is that it was confirmed to have leaked from Sohu. This time, the research institution actually used a similar method to.

# :34 飞书群里的完整链接

conduct their test. The lead researcher is named HDM. He sent out a pile of messages, about 2 million, each containing a unique, randomly generated URL that would never be used again. It’s the exact same concept as the " Zhang Sohu,""Li Taobao," and "Wang Jingdong" examples we just mentioned. The result was that these one-time URLs sent to Minimax were visited again after.

# :04 什么记录要留六个月

a period of time, such as several dozen hours later. Since these URLs were randomly generated and never used except when inputting them, if anyone visits them, it means there is a leak—just like someone calling to ask for Zhang Sohu; it's exactly the same. Throughout the test, they evaluated multiple AIs. Only the Minimax group had these URLs visited by third parties multiple times —anywhere from 40 to 130 hours after the.

# :29 资料转手后找谁删

initial request, with the latest being over five days later. So, why were these URLs visited? People speculate that Minimax might have some background URL scanning feature, meaning once someone asks about a URL, they scan it to verify it, store it, or perhaps use that data for other purposes . They switched to other service providers to continue using the Minimax model and.

# :23 让助手干活会暴露什么

found that this issue still persisted. We need to explain a few concepts here: first is OpenRouter, which is a token aggregator that does not have its own servers. The so-called Minimax or other services you purchase on it are handled by other token aggregators; however, some aggregators have their own servers and promise zero data retention. I deploy and operate the Minimax model inference here myself to ensure data.

# :24 亏损能证明卖数据吗

security for you, so these testers will test the Minimax services provided by different vendors. After discovering these issues, they would ask these API transit hubs—the vendors that built their own cloud services—what's going on, and why they didn't honor their promise of zero data retention? Why would you still be accessing a URL I gave you four or five days later? What exactly are you trying to do? Then they would say, "We had a routing error, we're terribly sorry."

# :15 我会怎么选模型

Originally, I should have finished serving you here, and I did promise zero data retention, but because Minimax was cheaper and faster, I routed your request over there. So, you can't entirely blame Minimax for this; the intermediaries acting as API transit hubs likely have issues as well . After such a report came out, OpenRouter , the world's largest API transit hub that doesn't own its own servers, definitely had to take action, right?

# :30 我为什么对自部署改口

They had no choice but to delist the suppliers—those providing computing power for Minimax—and revoke their zero-data-retention (ZDR) licenses directly. They've cut ties with three providers so far, and the number of service endpoints stripped of zero-retention status is 125. Everyone take note: the service prices offered by Chinese large model vendors vary; they are usually cheaper in mainland China and slightly more expensive overseas. So , these API transit hubs will try to find ways to create fake endpoints to route your traffic to mainland China instead.

# :10 点发送前我会想什么

These servers are categorized into: The first type is servers leased by Minimax in the China region. The second type is Minimax's official servers leased overseas, which use Minimax's own servers directly; the third type is servers deployed by other vendors using Minimax's open-source models. There are three types of servers. Minimax itself doesn't actually promise zero data retention; it's these third parties that say, "Once we deploy Minimax, we make this promise,. guaranteeing that when your data reaches us, it is not retained." But these people often cut corners; they route requests intended for their own inference services back and forth, and that's that. Routed to other servers of MX. MX's other servers could be abroad, or they could be in China; that's really ...Hard to say. This time, the tester specifically chose to request services from a US provider, and even selected one with a. zero-retention tag to handle the traffic . As a result, after 24 days, the full URL appeared in a Feishu group. Why was it discovered in a Feishu group ? Because links clicked within a Feishu group go through a special redirect, allowing you to know the click came from Feishu, and from devices in Beijing and Shanghai—accessed on three computers and three phones within two minutes. This essentially tears the mask off these token relay stations completely. Any claims like "I guarantee I use my own US-bought servers and deployed the open-source model myself" are nonsense; someone can still dig the full URL out of old logs. It effectively means that once you've used it, your traces remain forever, impossible to erase. In this instance, the link was indeed clicked from within China, on devices in. Beijing and Shanghai, and through a Feishu group. Now, OpenRouter's warning letter has named the MX route, but who this Feishu group belongs to hasn't been made clear . For instance, whether it's the Feishu used by MX itself or by another company , we don't know. What happens if your requests are actually routed there? Chinese law has requirements; first, to provide services to mainland China, you.

must commit to being legal and compliant . When I use MX's service in China, it often tells me, "Sorry, I can't do this ." Why? Because it deems what I said inappropriate; it follows the rules of its operator, and MX's compliance requirements are relatively high. It might not answer questions that others might. Looking further at China's requirements for information retention, "zero data retention" is illegal in China. This can only be achieved abroad; it is not permitted in China. First, let's look at the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services. Article 11 states that service providers must protect user input and usage records. You cannot collect unnecessary personal information, inputs that identify users , or usage records, nor can you store them illegally. There is a key term here called " illegal retention." It’s not that companies can just store whatever they want; the law doesn't say that. If you store too much, that is a problem . This is a corresponding regulation in China, as we also protect privacy. The second law is the Cybersecurity Law , which requires network logs to be kept for six months. The information you chat about with AI, and the content it returns to you, must be saved for six months as required by China's Cybersecurity Law; you cannot delete them during that time. If something illegal occurs, they might come to request these records. If you can't provide them, you will be fined. If the content you input contains illegal material, what happens then? They will stop, handle, and report it. I often encounter "stop"—that is, when I ask it to do some work, it says, "Sorry , I won't do that." As for "handle," I haven't encountered that yet, and as for whether I've been reported? Oh my, that is actually a bit scary. Perhaps some instructions I gave to MiniMax have already been reported to the relevant authorities. This guy often asks some very strange. questions, and I don't even know what he's trying to say. That is still a bit frightening. So, according to China's Cybersecurity Law, if MiniMax discovers that a user is engaging in illegal activities while using the service, it must save the relevant records, report them to the relevant departments, and stop you immediately. Then, which law might have triggered this incident? The "Interim Measures" mention services provided to the domestic public, and.

providing them via API can also be counted as an overseas request. Who is actually being served, and which obligation requires you to retain this data? Normal requests should be deleted after being answered. Inform customers about cases where retention is required by law. Auditing and zero-retention can technically coexist, but in China, you shouldn't claim zero-retention. If you normally keep everyone's questions and audit them in batches. after a few days, you must make that clear and let the customer choose. This is something MiniMax itself should handle; for all the questions you send, as long as they contain URLs, it will audit them itself after a few days. Now there is something even more troublesome than it keeping records for auditing. These data have already been passed around who knows where. If you wanted to delete them now, you wouldn't even know who to ask. What would happen if you used a Chinese model? Let me give you an example. I. went to the dentist a couple of days ago , and right after that, a bunch of dental clinics started calling me. They’d say, "Come get your teeth replaced here, we have a discount on dental implants." Don’t many people have this kind of life experience? Or, let’s say I clicked on a real estate ad today. Then a bunch of real estate agents call you up saying, "Oh, look how great our properties are," or something like that. My family also gets constant calls every day asking if my child needs to attend a tutoring center. I keep telling them repeatedly that my child is already in college and doesn't. need that. But it’s pointless. Why does this happen? It’s because the data was sold. And the people selling this data don't take any responsibility for its quality . Even if my child is already in college, they still keep my name on the list and sell it to these tutoring agencies. Because they charge based on the number of names—so much for 100 names, so much for 1,000. Whether the name is still valid or the. phone number is still in service, they don't care, because. This belongs to a gray market. No one can really explain where the data we give to MIMX actually goes. So it's possible that after chatting with MIMX for a while, they start calling you. You know what’s most annoying for me every year? It’s when I need to renew my car insurance, since you have to renew it annually. People keep calling non-stop, saying, "Oh, it's time to renew your car insurance, isn't it?" I tell them I’ve already sold my car,.

but it doesn't matter; they keep calling anyway because they bought that data, and you have no idea where to go to get them to delete it. Now, when we chat with large models and have AI do our work, it’s much more troublesome than when we used to register accounts like Zhang's Weibo, Li's Taobao, or Wang's JD. Why? Because the data that a place like Weibo could actually collect is very limited. At most, you just registered a user account, completed real-name verification, and entered your phone number. Listen everyone, all user accounts created in China require. identity verification and a linked mobile phone number. Once you've filled that out, you really can't do much on a search website; you might click a few pages or chat with someone, so the user data and behavior you leave behind isn't actually that much. But think about it, what will you do with AI? You will do everything with AI. You'll tell it, "Help me find a dentist ,""I'm looking at this car, help me research it," or "Help me look into houses in this area"—you'll tell it everything. Once you've said those things, it can. take all that data, including what you input and what it outputs, mine it, and then sell it. So, do you think Minimax would do that? Oh boy, Minimax is actually quite broke . Look, in the first half of 2024, they lost $ 358 million, leaving them with $ 1.323 billion in cash. How much longer can they burn through that? It’s hard to say, but the remaining money won't last very long. Look at their stock price again. On October 20th, it dropped 10.8%. You can look up the stock price and losses, but of course, you need hard evidence for the data-selling claims. But for me, why would I need hard evidence? Looking at their financial statements and their overall stock price, it really feels like desperation is setting in, right? Asking them to follow strict data protection rules is indeed a bit of a high expectation. So, how should I choose which model to use? First of all, try to use overseas models as much as possible, like OpenAI or Anthropic—though I can't use Anthropic anymore, so I'm stuck with OpenAI. If you insist on using Chinese models, try your best to deploy them yourself in a trusted environment. Don't trust those so-called intermediary service providers who say, "I bought the computing power, I'll deploy it for you "—don't believe that. There's absolutely no way to verify it. Think about it: their "zero data retention" promise was.

up for over half a year, then suddenly they canceled it. Those who used it in the meantime must be feeling pretty cold . Another thing is, never, ever put sensitive information in there, such as your clients 'phone numbers, your own specific details, or your account passwords—definitely, definitely don't put those in. If you send something like this to OpenAI or Claude, they will warn you not to send it over because it is very dangerous. You can also trust them with a high. probability that this content won't be stored locally. But if you send this to domestic models , you might get a surprise or a shock—I think it’s more likely to be a shock. I used to advise everyone not to deploy these models themselves. Today, I might have to go back on my word. If you really have AI inference needs, you may genuinely need to deploy private models in a controlled environment. All these token relay sites that you can use directly online are untrustworthy, especially those that route to China. Even if you say, "Can I just route to Claude through an API relay?" sometimes they might engage in bait-and-switch tactics. You think you’re using Claude. But it turns out DeepSeek or Kimi is doing the work for you, which is entirely possible. The recent exposure isn't really about Chinese models; these model providers in. China are subject to Chinese law. They are required to retain information and process reports when encountering illegal content; that is exactly what Chinese law mandates. What was truly exposed this time are these relay sites that claimed to use open-source Chinese models, stating they had deployed servers in the U.S. and guaranteed compliance with zero-data-retention requirements, but in reality, they secretly routed these service requests to China. This led Chinese providers to receive strange links, which they then verified , only to be caught red-handed by U.S. security agencies. This is the underlying logic of what actually happened. Let me summarize. The real issue this time isn't the Chinese large models, but the intermediary service providers. And since OpenRouter issued the warning letter, it proves that the providers connected under OpenRouter are equally unreliable.

I certainly don't want to chat with an AI about dental implants today, only to have someone call me tomorrow asking if I need to get my teeth filled. I’m talking about this today to remind everyone that when we use large AI models, we must always keep one thing in mind: who am I actually using? What exactly am I doing? What exactly have I told them? In case of a data leak, we need to know exactly where it leaked from. The models are here; I suggest everyone take a moment to think before hitting. that send button. But what if I'm just too lazy to put in that effort? Then go use GPT; there’s no other way. In the end, it just proves the old saying: they look down on me, and I just can't seem to step up. Alright. That’s the story for today. Thanks for listening. Please like, hit the notification bell, join our Discord , and we also welcome those who are interested and able to join our paid channel. Goodbye. Yeah.
